props.title: Some Kind of Wonderful
props.initialSlug: Teen mechanic pursues dream girl, finds true love

sections.content: Some Kind of Wonderful (1987) stands as John Hughes' spiritual successor to Pretty in Pink (1986), flipping the class dynamics with working-class Keith (Eric Stoltz) pursuing popular rich girl Amanda Jones (Lea Thompson). But it's Mary Stuart Masterson's Watts - the tomboy drummer hopelessly in love with her best friend Keith - who steals the show. The film crystallizes Hughes' signature blend of class consciousness and teen romance that defined 80s coming-of-age cinema, alongside works like Say Anything (1989) and Valley Girl (1983).

sections.content: Director Howard Deutch (who also helmed Pretty in Pink) brings Hughes' screenplay to life with authentic teen performances and a killer soundtrack featuring March Violets and Jesus and Mary Chain. The film's exploration of class barriers and unrequited love resonates with other key 80s teen films like The Breakfast Club (1985) and Lucas (1986), but stands apart through its grittier portrayal of working-class life and Masterson's groundbreaking portrayal of a gender non-conforming character.

The film's lasting influence can be seen in later teen romances that subvert expectations, from 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) to Easy A (2010). Its authentic depiction of teenage friendship-turned-romance laid groundwork for films like Perks of Being a Wallflower (2012) and Edge of Seventeen (2016), while its class-conscious narrative echoes through works like Lady Bird (2017). sections.content: While not as commercially successful as other Hughes films like Sixteen Candles (1984) or Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986), Some Kind of Wonderful has gained cult status for its honest portrayal of teenage emotions and class dynamics. The chemistry between Stoltz and Masterson influenced countless "friends-to-lovers" narratives, while Thompson's nuanced portrayal of Amanda Jones avoided the typical "popular mean girl" trope that dominated 80s teen cinema.
